findings.body: `execSync` runs the command through a shell, so the interpolated `userName` has to be assembled into a string and then re-parsed by `/bin/sh`. The previous `spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName])` form did the same job without a shell process, without any string building, and without quoting concerns. The extra `command` local and the shell hop are pure overhead over the argv form the standard library already offers.
findings.title: Pass arguments as an argv array instead of building a shell command string

findings.body: Swapping the import from `spawnSync` to `execSync` forces every call site in this module onto the shell-string form. Unless a shell feature (pipes, globbing, redirection) is actually needed here, `spawnSync` remains the appropriate API and keeping the import avoids the string-building indirection introduced below.
findings.title: Keep the child_process import on the argv-based API

findings.body: `rows.slice(1)` allocates a new array and silently discards the first row, while nothing else in the change explains or uses that truncation. It reads as a leftover from editing this function, and it also makes the function's contract ("render the given rows") no longer match what it returns.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller passing N rows receives N-1: the first row of every report is dropped from the output.
findings.title: Return the rows unchanged instead of slicing off the first element

findings.body: `toBeDefined()` passes for any non-undefined value, so the test no longer covers what `renderReport` returns and stops exercising the row handling that was just changed. The previous equality assertion was the only check that the rows survive the call; with it gone, the truncation introduced in `report.ts` goes unnoticed.
findings.title: Assert the returned rows rather than only that a value exists

The rewrite awaits `repository.load(id)` once per id inside a sequential loop, so the round-trip count scales with `ids.length` and each await blocks the next. findings.failure_scenario: A caller supplies an id with no corresponding record; `load` returns `None`, `item.active` raises AttributeError, and the request fails with a 500 whose presence/absence lets the caller probe for valid ids.
findings.suggestion: if item is not None and item.active:

findings.body: The batched `repo.load_many(ids)` call is replaced with one `repo.load(*id)` round trip per element of the caller-supplied `ids` slice, and nothing in the changed code limits how many elements that slice may hold. Each additional id now costs a separate backend round trip instead of a single batched one, so the work an attacker can trigger scales linearly with the size of the input they submit (N+1 amplification). If no length cap is enforced by the caller, add an explicit bound here (or keep the batched load) so a single large `ids` payload cannot occupy the service for an unbounded time. Also worth checking: `repo.load` returns an `Item` by value here, so any not-found/error case presumably panics or is handled inside the repo — the batch version had no such per-item failure mode.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller submits a request carrying a very large `ids` list; `enrich` issues one backend query per id instead of a single batched query, saturating the connection pool and stalling other requests until the loop finishes.
